Date and oat energy balls: 10 pitted dates
Soak the dates in warm water for 10 minutes and drain.
Add the dates, tahini and cinnamon and pulse until the mixture comes together.
With wet hands, shape walnut-sized balls.
Roll the balls in coconut and chill in the fridge for 30 minutes.
A handy snack you can eat with one hand while breastfeeding.
For young children grind the walnuts very finely; whole nuts are a choking risk.
Serve as a snack with tea or milk.
Keeps 1 week in a closed container in the fridge; 1 month in the freezer.
Spinach lentil salad
2 handfuls fresh spinach
Wash and finely chop the spinach; dice the pepper small and chop the parsley.
Whisk the lemon juice, olive oil and cumin to make a dressing.
Mix the warm lentils with the vegetables and add the dressing.
Adjust the salt and let rest for 10 minutes.
Lemon’s vitamin C boosts iron absorption from lentils; a good choice in pregnancy and the postpartum period.
Adding the dressing while warm helps the flavour soak in.
Baked salmon and vegetable tray
8 cherry tomatoes
Preheat the oven to 200°C; line the tray with baking paper.
Cut the zucchini and pepper into large pieces; leave the tomatoes whole.
Toss the vegetables with half the olive oil and the thyme and spread on the tray; bake for 10 minutes.
Place the salmon among the vegetables and drizzle with the remaining oil and lemon juice.
Bake for 12–15 minutes, until the salmon flakes easily and is opaque inside.
In pregnancy always cook fish thoroughly; avoid raw or undercooked fish.
Salmon is a good omega-3 source while breastfeeding; 2 portions of fish a week are recommended.
Serve hot with bulgur pilaf or a green salad.
Keeps 1 day in a closed container in the fridge.
Postpartum sherbet (homemade)
2 cinnamon sticks
5 cloves
1 small piece ginger
Put the water, cinnamon, cloves and ginger in a pot and bring to a boil.
Simmer on low heat for 10 minutes until the spices release their colour.
Add the sugar, stir until dissolved and boil 2 more minutes.
Strain and serve warm or cold.
You can reduce the sugar; if you had gestational diabetes, ask your doctor.
Drink spiced drinks in moderation while breastfeeding; pause if you notice the baby is unsettled.
Offer to guests warm or cold.
Keeps 3 days in a closed bottle in the fridge.
Kefir banana oat smoothie
1 tablespoon flaxseed
Put the oats and flaxseed in the blender with the kefir and wait 5 minutes.
Slice the banana and add it.
Add the cinnamon and blend for 30–40 seconds until smooth.
If too thick, add a little water or milk and blend again.
Flaxseed and kefir may help with constipation, common in pregnancy; also drink more water daily.
Using frozen banana makes it colder and creamier.
Drink immediately after making.
Don't let it stand; consume fresh.
One-pan vegetable bulgur pilaf
Chop the onion finely, and the carrot and zucchini into small cubes.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and sauté the onion for 3 minutes; add the carrot and cook 3 more minutes.
Add the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute, then add the zucchini and bulgur and mix.
Add the hot water and salt; once it boils, cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes.
Whole-grain bulgur is rich in fibre and keeps you full.
Set aside the child's portion before adding salt.
Serve with yoghurt or cacık.
Baked yoghurt chicken (family with kids)
Grate the garlic; mix with the yoghurt, olive oil and spices.
Coat the chicken in the sauce and marinate in the fridge for at least 30 minutes; then wash your hands and the chopping board.
Preheat the oven to 200°C and arrange the chicken on the tray.
Bake for 30–35 minutes, until the internal temperature reaches 75°C and the juices run clear.
Cut the child's portion into small strips; salt only the adult portion.
The longer it marinates, the softer the chicken; you can leave it overnight.
Serve hot with bulgur pilaf and salad.
Baked sweet potato with chickpeas
2 medium sweet potatoes
Wash the sweet potatoes and cut into cubes with the skin on.
Toss the potatoes and chickpeas with olive oil, cumin and paprika and spread in a single layer.
Bake for 25–30 minutes, until the potatoes are soft and the edges browned; stir halfway.
Serve topped with yoghurt.
Sweet potato provides vitamin A; chickpeas provide fibre and protein.
For children, mash or halve the chickpeas.
Serve warm; a green salad goes well alongside.
Walnut and dried apricot oat cookies
6 dried apricots
Preheat the oven to 180°C; line the tray with baking paper.
Mash the bananas with a fork and mix with the olive oil.
Finely chop the apricots and walnuts.
Mix all the ingredients and let rest for 10 minutes.
Drop spoonfuls onto the tray and press lightly; bake 15–18 minutes until the edges brown.
No sugar is added; the sweetness comes from banana and apricot.
Dried apricots contain iron; suitable as a snack in pregnancy.
Once completely cool, serve with milk or tea.
Keeps 4 days in an airtight container.
Vegetable omelette roll
30 g white cheese
Grate the zucchini and squeeze out the juice; dice the pepper small and chop the dill.
Whisk the eggs and milk; add the vegetables and crumbled cheese.
Heat a non-stick pan with a little oil and pour in the mixture as a thin layer.
Cook covered on low heat for 5–6 minutes, until the top is completely set.
Roll up with a spatula and slice.
In pregnancy cook eggs until both yolk and white are fully set.
The slices are easy for young children to hold.
Serve hot with tomato and cucumber.
Eat right away; at most 1 day in the fridge.
